question: Why ought you to glorify God?
answer: Because he made me and takes care of me.
right_choice: Because he made me and takes care of me.
wrong_choices: Because it makes us happy | Because He will reward those who obey | Because the Church requires it
audit_why: The catechism answer is right and matches Psalm 100:3, but the question had no Bible reference, so Ps 100:3 was added.

question: Are there more gods than one?
In how many persons does this one God exist?
wrong_choices: In countless manifestations | In seven spiritual forms | In two persons
audit_why: The catechism answer (three persons) is right, but the question had no reference, so I added Matthew 3:16-17 and 2 Corinthians 13:14, where Father, Son and Holy Spirit appear together.

question: What are they?
answer: The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
right_choice: The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
wrong_choices: The Father, the Son, and the Angel Gabriel | The Power, the Love, and the Wisdom of God | The Father, the Son, and the Virgin Mary

question: What is God?
answer: God is a Spirit, and has not a body like men.
right_choice: God is a Spirit, and has not a body like men.

question: Where is God?
wrong_choices: God is only in heaven, far above the earth | God is present only in holy places | God is only in the hearts of believers

question: Can you see God?

question: Does God know all things?
answer: Yes; nothing can be hid from God.
right_choice: Yes; nothing can be hid from God.
wrong_choices: Yes, only the important matters | Yes, but not our free choices | Yes, but not the future

question: Can God do all things?
answer: Yes; God can do all his holy will.
right_choice: Yes; God can do all his holy will.
wrong_choices: No; some things are too hard even for God. | No; God can do only what is easy. | Yes; God can do whatever people ask of him.

question: Where do you learn how to love and obey God?
wrong_choices: In the Bible and Church tradition | In philosophy and human reason | In the teachings of wise men

question: Who wrote the Bible?
answer: Holy men who were taught by the Holy Ghost.

question: Who were our first parents?
wrong_choices: Noah and his wife | Abraham and Sarah | Cain and Abel
audit_why: The answer is right and the choices are fair, but the question had no Bible reference, so I added Genesis 2:7, 21-22 and 3:20.

question: Of what were our first parents made?
answer: God made the body of Adam out of the ground, and formed Eve from the body of Adam.

question: What did God give Adam and Eve besides bodies?

question: Have you a soul as well as a body?
answer: Yes; I have a soul that can never die.
right_choice: Yes; I have a soul that can never die.
wrong_choices: Yes, but my soul will perish at death | Yes, my soul is my mind and will | Yes; my soul will enter another body when I die

question: How do you know that you have a soul?
answer: Because I can think about God and the world to come.
right_choice: Because I can think about God and the world to come.
wrong_choices: Because I can see, hear, and feel with my body. | Because I can eat, drink, and grow each day. | Because I can walk, run, and play with others.
audit_why: The catechism's answer is kept, but the wrong choices also described the soul, so they were replaced with things that belong to the body and are the same length as the right answer.

question: In what condition did God make Adam and Eve?
answer: He made them holy and happy.
right_choice: He made them holy and happy.
wrong_choices: He made them sinful and in need of a Savior | He made them perfect in all knowledge | He made them strong and wealthy

question: What is a covenant?

right_choice: An agreement between two or more persons.
wrong_choices: A gathering of people for worship | A law established by divine authority | A promise made by God to mankind
audit_why: One wrong choice, "A bond created by mutual consent," says nearly the same thing as the catechism's answer, so I replaced it with a choice that is clearly wrong.

question: What covenant did God make with Adam?
wrong_choices: The Mosaic covenant | The covenant of grace | The covenant of obedience

question: What was Adam bound to do by the covenant of works?
wrong_choices: To offer sacrifices for sin | To trust in a promised Savior | To repent and be forgiven
audit_why: Three wrong choices were also true of Adam's duty (loving God, keeping the commandments, working the garden), so they were replaced with things that belong to the covenant of grace or to fallen people, and the reference Gen 2:16-17 was added.

question: What did God promise in the covenant of works?
answer: To reward Adam with life if he obeyed him.

wrong_choices: To give Adam's children a land forever | To forgive Adam if he repented of sin | To save Adam through a promised Savior
audit_why: Two wrong choices were nearly the same as the catechism's answer of life for obedience, and the third was true elsewhere in Genesis, so all three were replaced with clearly wrong choices, and the reference Genesis 2:16-17 was added.

question: What did God threaten in the covenant of works?
answer: To punish Adam with death if he disobeyed.
right_choice: To punish Adam with death if he disobeyed.
wrong_choices: To remove Adam's dominion over creation | To cause Adam great suffering and pain | To cast Adam out of the garden
audit_why: The question and answer match Genesis 2:17 ("you will surely die"), but the question had no Bible reference, so Gen 2:16-17 was added.

question: Did Adam keep the covenant of works?
wrong_choices: Yes; he obeyed God in everything | Yes; only Eve broke God's command | Yes; he kept it until he died
audit_why: The wrong choices all described Adam's sin and so were also true, so they were replaced with choices saying he kept the covenant, and the Genesis 3 reference was added.

question: What is meant by want of conformity?
answer: Not being or doing what God requires.
right_choice: Not being or doing what God requires.
wrong_choices: Not knowing what God has said. | Being tempted to do wrong. | Doing what God forbids.
audit_why: The three wrong choices all said almost the same thing as the right answer, so I replaced them with choices that are clearly different: transgression (doing what God forbids), ignorance, and temptation.

question: What is meant by transgression?
wrong_choices: Being born with a sinful nature | Being punished for our sins | Not doing what God requires
audit_why: Two of the wrong choices were just other ways of saying "doing what God forbids", and the third was too close to it, so they now give clearly different ideas, including the catechism's own contrast, "not doing what God requires".

question: What was the sin of our first parents?
Who tempted them to this sin?
answer: The devil tempted Eve, and she gave the fruit to Adam.

question: What befell our first parents when they had sinned?
answer: Instead of being holy and happy, they became sinful and miserable.

question: Did Adam act for himself alone in the covenant of works?
answer: No; he represented all his posterity.

wrong_choices: No; he acted as a priest for mankind | No; he represented all creation | No; he represented only those who would believe

question: What effect had the sin of Adam on all mankind?
answer: All mankind are born in a state of sin and misery.

question: What is that sinful nature which we inherit from Adam called?
wrong_choices: Sin of omission | Actual sin | The unpardonable sin
audit_why: The three wrong choices were all other ways of saying "original sin", so they were replaced with different kinds of sin, and Romans 5:12 was added as the reference.

question: What does every sin deserve?
answer: The wrath and curse of God.

question: Can any one go to heaven with this sinful nature?
answer: No, our hearts must be changed before we can be fit for heaven.

question: What is a change of heart called?
wrong_choices: Justification | Sanctification | Adoption

question: Who can change a sinner's heart?
wrong_choices: God the Father alone | Jesus Christ alone | A faithful pastor

question: Can any one be saved through the covenant of works?

question: Why can none be saved through the covenant of works?
answer: Because all have broken it, and are condemned by it.

question: With whom did God the Father make the covenant of grace?

audit_why: One wrong choice ("all believers in Christ") is close to the fuller teaching that the covenant is in Christ for his people, so it was replaced, and the reference 2 Timothy 1:9 was added.

question: Whom did Christ represent in the covenant of grace?
wrong_choices: The faithful and righteous | All who hear the gospel | The Jewish nation only

question: What did Christ undertake in the covenant of grace?
answer: To keep the whole law for his people, and to suffer the punishment due to their sins.

audit_why: The three wrong choices all described Christ's work in nearly the same words as the catechism's answer, so I replaced them with choices that clearly differ from keeping the law and bearing the penalty for his people.

question: Did our Lord Jesus Christ ever commit the least sin?

question: How could the Son of God suffer?

audit_why: The catechism answer is right, but the wrong choices were also true things the Bible says about Christ and were longer than the right one, so I replaced them with clearly wrong ones of similar length and added a reference.

question: What is meant by the Atonement?

question: What did God the Father undertake in the covenant of grace?

question: What is justification?

question: What is sanctification?

question: For whom did Christ obey and suffer?

question: What kind of life did Christ live on earth?

question: What kind of death did Christ die?

question: Who will be saved?

question: What is it to repent?

question: Can you repent and believe in Christ by your own power?

question: How can you get the help of the Holy Spirit?

question: About how long ago did Christ die?

question: How were pious persons saved before the coming of Christ?

question: How did pious persons before Christ show their faith in the Saviour to come?

question: What did these sacrifices represent?

question: What three offices does Christ have as our Redeemer?

question: How is Christ a prophet?

question: How is Christ a priest?

wrong_choices: God is merciful and will eventually excuse all sins, even serious ones against His majesty | God is just but His mercy means that all sins will be ultimately forgiven | God is merciful, therefore punishment for sin is temporary and limited in duration
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Since, according to God's righteous judgment we deserve temporal and eternal punishment, how can we escape this punishment and be again received into favour?
answer: God demands that His justice be satisfied. Therefore full payment must be made either by ourselves or by another.
right_choice: God demands that His justice be satisfied. Full payment must be made by ourselves or another.
wrong_choices: God's infinite mercy means His justice can be completely ignored and no payment needed | We alone must make full payment ourselves and cannot receive help from anyone | God will accept partial payment for our sins if we truly and sincerely repent
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Can we ourselves make this payment?
answer: Certainly not. On the contrary, we daily increase our debt.
right_choice: Certainly not. On the contrary, we daily increase our debt.
wrong_choices: No, but we can help Christ to make the payment | Yes, if we keep God's law faithfully from now on | No, our payment is impossible because our sins are infinite
audit_why: One wrong choice ("only Christ can make the perfect payment") is also true, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong choice; everything else is unchanged.

question: Can any mere creature pay for us?
answer: No. In the first place, God will not punish another creature for the sin which man has committed. Furthermore, no mere creature can sustain the burden of God's eternal wrath against sin and deliver others from it.
right_choice: No. God will not punish another creature for man's sin, nor can any creature sustain God's eternal wrath
wrong_choices: No, but the angels are powerful enough to bear and endure God's eternal wrath | Yes, God can punish an innocent creature for man's sin if He should choose | No, because God will simply forgive man's sin without any payment being required
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What kind of mediator and deliverer must we seek?
answer: One who is a true and righteous man, and yet more powerful than all creatures; that is, one who is at the same time true God.
right_choice: One who is a true and righteous man and also true God, more powerful than all creatures
wrong_choices: One who is a righteous angel or spirit, more powerful than humans but lesser than God | One who is truly God but need not necessarily be human or righteous | One who is human and filled with God's Holy Spirit but not truly God
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why must He be a true and righteous man?
answer: He must be a true man because the justice of God requires that the same human nature which has sinned should pay for sin. He must be a righteous man because one who himself is a sinner cannot pay for others.
right_choice: He must be truly human so human nature can pay for sin, and righteous so He can pay for others
wrong_choices: He must be human but need not be righteous, only willing to sacrifice Himself | He must be righteous but need not be human, as God's divine power alone is sufficient | He must be divine and powerful, but His righteousness depends on God's mercy and accounting
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why must He at the same time be true God?
answer: He must be true God so that by the power of His divine nature He might bear in His human nature the burden of God's wrath, and might obtain for us and restore to us righteousness and life.
right_choice: By His divine power He can bear God's wrath, obtaining and restoring for us righteousness and life
wrong_choices: By His divine mercy He forgave all sins and granted righteousness without bearing wrath | By His teachings He showed humanity how to bear God's wrath and gain eternal life | By His human nature alone He could endure God's wrath and obtain righteousness for us
audit_why: No fault found.

question: But who is that Mediator who at the same time is true God and a true and righteous man?
answer: Our Lord Jesus Christ, who became to us wisdom from God—our righteousness, holiness, and redemption.
right_choice: Our Lord Jesus Christ, who became to us wisdom from God, our righteousness, holiness, and redemption
wrong_choices: God the Father, who made all things and provides wisdom and redemption alone | The greatest human teacher who lived righteously and demonstrated the path to God | The Holy Spirit given by God to provide wisdom and sanctification to believers
audit_why: The answer quoted 1 Corinthians 1:30 in non-BSB wording ("sanctification", "whom God made"), so it now follows the BSB ("holiness", "who became to us wisdom from God"), and that verse is added to the references.

question: From where do you know this?
answer: From the holy gospel, which God Himself first revealed in Paradise. Later, He had it proclaimed by the patriarchs and prophets, and foreshadowed by the sacrifices and other ceremonies of the law. Finally, He had it fulfilled through His only Son.
right_choice: From the gospel: God revealed it in Paradise, proclaimed by patriarchs and prophets, foreshadowed in the law
wrong_choices: From personal experience and the wisdom of great men about how to find salvation | From the New Testament alone, which replaced the Old Testament and all its ancient prophecies | From the reasoning of Greek philosophers about the nature of God and man
audit_why: One wrong choice spoke of ancient prophets predicting the Messiah, which is also part of the catechism's answer, so I replaced it with a choice about Greek philosophers that is clearly wrong.

question: Are all men, then, saved by Christ just as they perished through Adam?
answer: No. Only those are saved who by a true faith are grafted into Christ and accept all His benefits.
right_choice: No. Only those are saved who by a true faith are grafted into Christ and accept all His benefits.
wrong_choices: Only those who have been baptized and properly received the church sacraments are truly saved | Yes, because Christ died for all humanity and therefore all people are saved through His death | No, some are saved by faith in Christ while others are saved by their good works
audit_why: No fault found.

question: According to the Heidelberg Catechism, what is true faith?
answer: True faith is a sure knowledge whereby I accept as true all that God has revealed to us in His Word. At the same time it is a firm confidence that not only to others, but also to me, God has granted forgiveness of sins, everlasting righteousness, and salvation, out of mere grace, only for the sake of Christ's merits. This faith the Holy Spirit works in my heart by the gospel.
right_choice: Sure knowledge of God's Word and firm confidence that Christ's merits save me by grace
wrong_choices: A feeling, produced by my own will, that God is pleased with me | Knowing that God exists, even as the demons believe, without personal trust in Him | A hope that God will forgive me if my good works outweigh my sins
audit_why: The catechism's answer is right, but "True/False" cannot answer "What is true faith?", so I gave a short form of the catechism's answer and three believable wrong choices.

question: What, then, must a Christian believe?
answer: All that is promised us in the Gospel, which the articles of our catholic and undoubted Christian faith teach us in a summary.
right_choice: All promised in the Gospel, which the articles of Christian faith teach in summary
wrong_choices: Whatever brings personal comfort and hope based on our individual understanding of Scripture | What the church has determined and declared to be necessary for all true Christians | Only those teachings of the apostles which are clearly and directly written in the Bible
audit_why: No fault found.

question: In the Apostles' Creed, how do we confess that Jesus Christ was conceived and born?
answer: He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.
right_choice: He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.
wrong_choices: Conceived by Joseph, born of the virgin Mary | Conceived by the angel Gabriel, born of Elizabeth | Conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of Joseph's wife Elizabeth
audit_why: The original answer was the whole Creed with stray numbering, and its choices were vague, overlapping lists; the question now asks about one article of the Creed, which Matthew 1:20-23 confirms, with clear wrong choices.

question: How are these articles divided?
answer: Into three parts: the first is about God the Father and our creation; the second about God the Son and our redemption; the third about God the Holy Spirit and our sanctification.
right_choice: Into three parts: God the Father and creation; God the Son and redemption; God the Holy Spirit and sanctification
wrong_choices: Into various parts based on each sacrament and how it individually applies to believers | Into two main parts: the teachings of the Old Testament and the New Testament faith | Into ten parts, one for each of the Ten Commandments and corresponding doctrine
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Since there is only one God, why do you speak of three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?
answer: Because God has so revealed Himself in His Word that these three distinct persons are the one, true, eternal God.
right_choice: Because God revealed in His Word that these three distinct persons are the one, true God
wrong_choices: Because the three persons represent different roles that God plays in salvation | Because human minds cannot comprehend one God, so we use three | Because the Father is God, but the Son and Spirit are not divine
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What do you believe when you say: I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth?
answer: That the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who out of nothing created heaven and earth and all that is in them, and who still upholds and governs them by His eternal counsel and providence, is, for the sake of Christ His Son, my God and my Father. In Him I trust so completely as to have no doubt that He will provide me with all things necessary for body and soul, and will also turn to my good whatever adversity He sends me in this life of sorrow. He is able to do so as almighty God, and willing also as a faithful Father.
right_choice: The eternal Father of Christ, Creator of all, who upholds all, is my God and Father in whom I trust
wrong_choices: God the Father is the Creator of all things, but it is Christ who upholds them | God the Father created all things long ago, but may not provide for our daily needs | The eternal Father has power over creation, but we should primarily trust our own ability
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What do you understand by the providence of God?
answer: God's providence is His almighty and ever present power, whereby, as with His hand, He still upholds heaven and earth and all creatures, and so governs them that leaf and blade, rain and drought, fruitful and barren years, food and drink, health and sickness, riches and poverty, indeed, all things, come not by chance but by His fatherly hand.
right_choice: God's almighty power by which He upholds all things and governs all creatures by His fatherly hand
wrong_choices: God's saving power by which He redeems His people and brings them safely to heaven | God's judging power by which He punishes the wicked and rewards the righteous in this life | God's creative power by which He made all things and then left them to run by themselves
audit_why: Two wrong choices (sovereign decree, foreknowledge) and "creative power that sustains" were so close to the catechism's answer that they could also be chosen, so I replaced them with clearly different ideas (God leaving creation alone, saving power, judging power).

question: What does it benefit us to know that God has created all things and still upholds them by His providence?
answer: We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and with a view to the future we can have a firm confidence in our faithful God and Father that no creature shall separate us from His love; for all creatures are so completely in His hand that without His will they cannot so much as move.
right_choice: We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and confident no creature shall separate us from His love.
wrong_choices: We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and assured that God's love remains certain if we are faithful. | We should be patient in adversity, obey God in prosperity, and demonstrate through our faithfulness that we truly trust Him. | We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and demonstrate our righteous standing before God through our sincere obedience.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why is the Son of God called Jesus, that is, Saviour?
answer: Because He saves us from all our sins, and because salvation is not to be sought or found in anyone else.
right_choice: Because He saves us from all our sins, and salvation is found in Him alone
wrong_choices: Because He was born in Nazareth, where Joseph and Mary made their home | Because the priests chose the name for Him at the temple in Jerusalem | Because He teaches us the way and example of how to live righteously before God
audit_why: Two wrong choices (His punishment-bearing and resurrection, and His ransom) also describe how Jesus saves, so they could be picked fairly; they were replaced with choices that clearly do not explain the name in Matthew 1:21.

question: Do those believe in the only Saviour Jesus who seek their salvation and well-being from saints, in themselves, or anywhere else?
answer: No. Though they boast of Him in words, they in fact deny the only Saviour Jesus. For one of two things must be true: either Jesus is not a complete Saviour, or those who by true faith accept this Saviour must find in Him all that is necessary for their salvation.
right_choice: No, they deny that Jesus is the complete Saviour in whom all necessary salvation must be found
wrong_choices: Yes, because saints may add what is lacking in what Jesus has done for salvation | Yes, provided they also trust their own good works for part of their salvation | Yes, since they still confess Jesus with their lips as their Saviour and Lord
audit_why: The three wrong choices all said "No" with reasons that were also true, so they were replaced with clearly wrong "Yes" answers; the question and answer are unchanged.

question: Why is He called Christ, that is, Anointed?
answer: Because He has been ordained by God the Father, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, to be our chief Prophet and Teacher, who has fully revealed to us the secret counsel and will of God concerning our redemption; our only High Priest, who by the one sacrifice of His body has redeemed us, and who continually intercedes for us before the Father; and our eternal King, who governs us by His Word and Spirit, and who defends and preserves us in the redemption obtained for us.
right_choice: As God's anointed, He is our Prophet revealing God's will, our Priest who redeemed us through sacrifice, and our eternal King
wrong_choices: As God's anointed, He is our Lawgiver like Moses, our Priest offering sacrifices yearly, and our King over Israel alone | As God's anointed, He is our Judge condemning sinners, our Scribe interpreting the law, and our Commander of armies | As God's anointed, He is our Prophet foretelling coming events, our Priest of the line of Aaron, and our earthly King
audit_why: The catechism's answer is sound, but the wrong choices were close synonyms of Prophet, Priest and King and only the right one echoed 'anointed', so I gave all choices the same opening and made the wrong ones clearly contrary to the teaching.

question: Why are you called a Christian?
answer: Because I am a member of Christ by faith and thus share in His anointing, so that I may as prophet confess His Name, as priest present myself a living sacrifice of thankfulness to Him, and as king fight with a free and good conscience against sin and the devil in this life, and hereafter reign with Him eternally over all creatures.
right_choice: Because I am a member of Christ by faith and share His anointing as prophet, priest, and king
wrong_choices: Because I attend church regularly and participate in its sacraments faithfully | Because I believe in the teachings of Christ and live a moral life | Because Christ called His followers Christians during His earthly ministry to them
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why is He called God's only begotten Son, since we also are children of God?
answer: Because Christ alone is the eternal, natural Son of God. We, however, are children of God by adoption, through grace, for Christ's sake.
right_choice: Because Christ alone is God's eternal natural Son, while we are children of God by adoption through grace
wrong_choices: Because Christ is God's Son by adoption through grace, while we are God's children by nature from birth | Because Christ is the only One born of God, while all believers become God's children at baptism | Because Christ became God's Son at His baptism, while we are God's children by nature through creation
audit_why: Two wrong choices were close to the catechism's own teaching (children of God through Christ's work, or through faith), so I replaced them with choices that clearly contradict it.

question: Why do you call Him our Lord?
answer: Because He has ransomed us, body and soul, from all our sins, not with silver or gold but with His precious blood, and has freed us from all the power of the devil to make us His own possession.
right_choice: Because He ransomed us, body and soul, from sin and the devil's power with His precious blood
wrong_choices: Because He taught us God's law, so that by keeping it we earn freedom from sin and the devil | Because He has authority over us as our supreme Master and demands our obedience and worship | Because He rewarded us for our good works, body and soul, with silver and gold and a place in heaven
audit_why: Two wrong choices described being bought, freed from darkness, or owned by creation, which are also true, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict the catechism's teaching of redemption by Christ's blood.

question: What do you confess when you say: He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary?
answer: The eternal Son of God, who is and remains true and eternal God, took upon Himself true human nature from the flesh and blood of the virgin Mary, through the working of the Holy Spirit. Thus He is also the true seed of David, and like His brothers in every respect, yet without sin.
right_choice: The eternal Son of God took on true human nature from the virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit, remaining true God, without sin
wrong_choices: The Son of God took true human nature from the virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit, but ceased to be God | The Son of God became human born of the virgin Mary to demonstrate that sinless living is always possible | Jesus received human nature from both Mary and Joseph, and became the Son of God only at His birth
audit_why: Two wrong choices were also acceptable (one said the same thing as the right answer, another was close to "God with us"), so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict the catechism and the Bible.

question: What benefit do you receive from the holy conception and birth of Christ?
answer: He is our Mediator, and with His innocence and perfect holiness covers, in the sight of God, my sin, in which I was conceived and born.
right_choice: He is our Mediator and with His innocence and perfect holiness covers my sin before God
wrong_choices: His innocent life shows us that sinless living is possible and teaches us how to overcome temptation | His holy birth and innocent life give us an example of perfect obedience and moral purity to imitate | His conception and birth in purity remove our guilt and enable us to become holy ourselves
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What do you confess when you say that He suffered?
answer: During all the time He lived on earth, but especially at the end, Christ bore in body and soul the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race. Thus, by His suffering, as the only atoning sacrifice, He has redeemed our body and soul from everlasting damnation, and obtained for us the grace of God, righteousness, and eternal life.
right_choice: That Christ bore God's wrath against the sin of humanity, and through His suffering as atoning sacrifice redeemed us
wrong_choices: That Christ experienced all our pain and sorrow to show His sympathy with our struggles and sorrows | That Christ bore all our sicknesses and pain so we could be physically and spiritually healed | That Christ suffered greatly throughout His life to show us how to endure persecution and hardship faithfully
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why did He suffer under Pontius Pilate as judge?
answer: Though innocent, Christ was condemned by an earthly judge, and so He freed us from the severe judgment of God that was to fall on us.
right_choice: Though innocent, Christ was condemned by an earthly judge, freeing us from God's severe judgment
wrong_choices: Christ was sentenced by human authority to teach us that obedience to God matters most | Christ was condemned by an earthly court to show us that innocent people sometimes suffer unjustly | Though innocent, Christ was judged by Pilate to teach us to endure unjust treatment with patience
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Does it have a special meaning that Christ was crucified and did not die in a different way?
answer: Yes. Thereby I am assured that He took upon Himself the curse which lay on me, for a crucified one was cursed by God.
right_choice: Yes. Thereby I am assured that He took upon Himself the curse which lay on me
wrong_choices: Yes. Thereby I am assured that Rome, not God, judged Him, so His cross carried no curse at all | No. Any other death would have won my pardon equally, since the manner of His dying made no difference | Yes. Thereby I am assured that He was the first martyr, whose example I must follow to be saved
audit_why: The wrong choices were all roughly true (shameful, for criminals, what our sins deserved), so I replaced them with choices that clearly contradict the catechism's teaching that Christ bore the curse of God for us.

question: Why was it necessary for Christ to humble Himself even unto death?
answer: Because of the justice and truth of God satisfaction for our sins could be made in no other way than by the death of the Son of God.
right_choice: Because God's justice and truth required that satisfaction for our sins be made only through death of God's Son
wrong_choices: Because Satan held a lawful claim over sinners, and God's justice required that Christ's death be paid to him | Because our own good works and repentance, joined to Christ's example, could satisfy God's justice for our sins | Because God's mercy allowed our sins to be forgiven without any satisfaction, and Christ died only to set us an example
audit_why: The three wrong choices all stated true teaching close to the catechism's answer, so I replaced them with choices that the catechism and the Bible clearly reject.

question: Why was he buried?
answer: His burial testified that He had really died.
right_choice: His burial testified that He had really died.
wrong_choices: To show that He was a criminal who deserved death | So His disciples would have a tomb to visit after | So that He would rise from the dead on the third day
audit_why: One wrong choice (fulfilling prophecy) is also true, since Isaiah 53:9 foretold His burial, so it was replaced with a choice that is clearly wrong.

question: Since Christ has died for us, why do we still have to die?
answer: Our death is not a payment for our sins, but it puts an end to sin and is an entrance into eternal life.
right_choice: Our death is not payment for our sins but ends sin and enters eternal life
wrong_choices: Our death is payment for the sins that Christ's death did not cover | Our death is a punishment that makes us worthy of eternal life | Our death is a cleansing of guilt that must happen before we enter heaven
audit_why: The three wrong choices were all true and close to the catechism's answer, so I replaced them with ideas the catechism and Scripture deny (death as payment, as merit, or as purifying).

question: What further benefit do we receive from Christ's sacrifice and death on the cross?
answer: Through Christ's death our old nature is crucified, put to death, and buried with Him, so that the evil desires of the flesh may no longer reign in us, but that we may offer ourselves to Him as a sacrifice of thankfulness.
right_choice: Through Christ's death our old nature is crucified with Him so we may offer ourselves as a sacrifice to Him
wrong_choices: Through Christ's death we gain power to overcome temptation and to live in righteousness always | Through Christ's death we are freed from all evil desires so we naturally love holiness | Through Christ's death our guilt is removed so we no longer need to struggle against sin
audit_why: One wrong choice (sinful flesh put to death, living for God's glory) was nearly the same as the catechism's answer, so I replaced it with a choice that wrongly says we no longer need to struggle against sin.

question: Why is there added: He descended into hell?
answer: In my greatest sorrows and temptations I may be assured and comforted that my Lord Jesus Christ, by His unspeakable anguish, pain, terror, and agony, which He endured throughout all His sufferings but especially on the cross, has delivered me from the anguish and torment of hell.
right_choice: So that through His unspeakable suffering and agony, especially on the cross, Christ delivered us from hell's torment
wrong_choices: That Christ preached to the lost in hell after His death to give them a second chance to repent | That Christ went to the place of the dead to free the righteous souls held captive there | That Christ warned us to fear hell so that we would live holy lives out of terror
audit_why: Two wrong choices described Christ bearing hell's torment or separation from God, which is nearly what the catechism teaches, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict it.

question: How does Christ's resurrection benefit us?
answer: First, by His resurrection He has overcome death, so that He could make us share in the righteousness which He had obtained for us by His death. Second, by His power we too are raised up to a new life. Third, Christ's resurrection is to us a sure pledge of our glorious resurrection.
right_choice: By His resurrection Christ overcame death, shares righteousness with us, raises us to new life, and pledges our glorious resurrection
wrong_choices: By His resurrection Christ replaced the need for faith, removed all temptation from believers, and guarantees an earthly kingdom now | By His resurrection Christ ended all earthly suffering for believers, made us righteous by our own works, and promises worldly prosperity | By His resurrection Christ merely proved His divinity, gave us an example to follow, and promises that only our souls will live on
audit_why: The catechism's answer is sound, but the wrong choices were true statements or nearly the same as the right one, so I replaced them with choices that clearly contradict the three benefits the catechism gives.

question: What do you confess when you say, He ascended into heaven?
answer: That Christ, before the eyes of His disciples, was taken up from the earth into heaven, and that He is there for our benefit until He comes again to judge the living and the dead.
right_choice: That Christ was taken up into heaven before His disciples and is there for our benefit until He comes to judge
wrong_choices: That Christ was taken up into heaven before His disciples and will never come back to earth again | That Christ was taken up into heaven before His disciples and there offers Himself again and again for us | That Christ was taken up into heaven in secret, unseen by His disciples, and is there for our benefit
audit_why: Three of the wrong choices were also true or nearly the same as the right answer (Christ interceding, preparing a place, awaiting judgment), so I replaced them with choices that contradict the Bible (Heb 9:25; Acts 1:9-11).

question: Is Christ, then, not with us until the end of the world, as He has promised us?
answer: Christ is true man and true God. With respect to His human nature He is no longer on earth, but with respect to His divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit He is never absent from us.
right_choice: By His divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit Christ is never absent from us; by His human nature He is no longer on earth.
wrong_choices: Christ is present on earth in His body in the bread and wine, though His divinity is only in heaven | Christ is no longer with us in any way, since He ascended to heaven and left the world behind | By His human nature Christ is still on earth everywhere, but by His divinity He is absent from us
audit_why: The three wrong choices all repeated the catechism's own teaching, so they were also right; I replaced them with choices that contradict it and tightened the right choice to say His human nature is "no longer on earth."

question: But are the two natures in Christ not separated from each other if His human nature is not present wherever His divinity is?
answer: Not at all, for His divinity has no limits and is present everywhere. So it must follow that His divinity is indeed beyond the human nature which He has taken on and nevertheless is within this human nature and remains personally united with it.
right_choice: His divinity has no limits, is present everywhere, and is personally united with His human nature.
wrong_choices: His divinity and humanity are completely separate natures not truly united in one person. | His human nature became unlimited and present everywhere after His ascension to heaven. | His divine nature alone is truly present everywhere; His human nature exists nowhere.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How does Christ's ascension into heaven benefit us?
answer: First, He is our Advocate in heaven before His Father. Second, we have our flesh in heaven as a sure pledge that He, our Head, will also take us, His members, up to Himself. Third, He sends us His Spirit as a counter-pledge, by whose power we seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God, and not the things that are on earth.
right_choice: Our Advocate in heaven; our flesh there pledges He will take us; Spirit sent enables us to seek heavenly things.
wrong_choices: Our King ruling the earth now; our souls there are kept while bodies perish; Spirit sent makes us seek earthly blessings. | Our Priest offering sacrifice daily; our good works there earn our reward; Spirit sent frees us from all earthly troubles. | Our Teacher in heaven; our prayers there reach Him through the saints; Spirit sent lets us rest from seeking things above.
audit_why: The three wrong choices just repeated the catechism's three benefits in other words, so they were also right; they now state things the catechism and Bible do not teach, and the reference is tidied.

question: Why is it added, And sits at the right hand of God?
answer: Christ ascended into heaven to manifest Himself there as Head of His Church, through whom the Father governs all things.
right_choice: Christ ascended to manifest Himself as Head of His Church, through whom the Father governs all things.
wrong_choices: Christ ascended to leave His human nature behind so that only His divine nature remained in heaven | Christ ascended to rest from His work and hand the governing of all things over to the Church | Christ ascended to be separated from the earth and to await His return as judge of all
audit_why: Two wrong choices said Christ reigns in glory over all creation, which the Bible also teaches, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict the catechism's answer.

question: How does the glory of Christ, our Head, benefit us?
answer: First, by His Holy Spirit He pours out heavenly gifts upon us, His members. Second, by His power He defends and preserves us against all enemies.
right_choice: By His Spirit He pours out heavenly gifts; by His power He defends us against all enemies.
wrong_choices: By His example He shows us how to live; by His wisdom He helps us earn a place in heaven | By His Spirit He makes us perfectly holy now; by His power He frees us from all suffering in this life | By His blood He pays for our sins; by His power He gives us worldly wealth and success
audit_why: The right answer matches the Heidelberg Catechism, but the old wrong choices were also true or nearly the same (sanctifying us, guarding His church), so I replaced them with choices that clearly differ from the catechism's teaching.

question: What comfort is it to you that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead?
answer: In all my sorrow and persecution I lift up my head and eagerly await as judge from heaven the very same person who before has submitted Himself to the judgment of God for my sake, and has removed all the curse from me. He will cast all His and my enemies into everlasting condemnation, but He will take me and all His chosen ones to Himself into heavenly joy and glory.
right_choice: Christ, who bore God's judgment for me, will judge my enemies and bring me to glory.
wrong_choices: Christ will return to judge all humanity impartially and assign eternal rewards or punishments accordingly | Christ will examine all people's deeds and determine who deserves heaven based on their moral goodness | Christ will judge all people fairly based on their works, rewarding the good and punishing the evil
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What do you believe concerning the Holy Spirit?
answer: First, He is, together with the Father and the Son, true and eternal God. Second, He is also given to me, to make me by true faith share in Christ and all His benefits, to comfort me, and to remain with me forever.
right_choice: He is true eternal God with Father and Son; given to share Christ with me, comfort me, and remain forever.
wrong_choices: He is the highest of God's creatures; given to teach us, comfort us, and stay with us for a time | He is God's power at work in the world; given to make us holy and to guide our decisions | He is true God; given to enable our faith in Christ, to strengthen us, and to remain in our hearts
audit_why: The catechism answer is right, but one wrong choice was nearly the same as it, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong one (the Spirit as a created being who stays only for a time), and the reference was put in standard form.

question: What do you believe concerning the holy catholic Christian church?
answer: I believe that the Son of God, out of the whole human race, from the beginning of the world to its end, gathers, defends, and preserves for Himself, by His Spirit and Word, in the unity of the true faith, a church chosen to everlasting life. And I believe that I am and forever shall remain a living member of it.
right_choice: Christ gathers the church from all time through His Spirit and Word in true faith, and I'm a living member.
wrong_choices: Christ founded the church to teach the ways of salvation and to bring all people into His kingdom | Christ established the church as His body with a visible structure and leadership for all the faithful to follow | The church is the people whom Christ calls to worship together and to serve Him through loving others
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What do you understand by the communion of saints?
answer: First, that believers, all and everyone, as members of Christ have communion with Him and share in all His treasures and gifts. Second, that everyone is duty-bound to use his gifts readily and cheerfully for the benefit and well-being of the other members.
right_choice: Believers as Christ's members share in His treasures and gifts; everyone must use their gifts for others' benefit.
wrong_choices: Believers who have died as saints intercede for the living; everyone must pray to them for help | Only the most holy believers share in Christ's treasures; the rest must earn a share by their own good works | All Christians share the same spiritual gifts and blessings through their union with Christ in the church
audit_why: Two wrong choices were so close to the catechism's answer that they could fairly be picked, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict it and the Bible (1 Cor 12:4-13; Rom 12:4-8).

question: What do you believe concerning the forgiveness of sins?
answer: I believe that God, because of Christ's satisfaction, will no more remember my sins, nor my sinful nature, against which I have to struggle all my life, but He will graciously grant me the righteousness of Christ, that I may never come into condemnation.
right_choice: God won't remember my sins or sinful nature against me but grants me Christ's righteousness so I never face condemnation.
wrong_choices: God forgives my sins but still holds my sinful nature against me until I have overcome it by my own effort | God covers my sins with Christ's blood and then enables me to become righteous through faithful obedience | God forgives my past sins through Christ, but I must earn forgiveness for my later sins by my own good works
audit_why: The catechism answer is sound, but two wrong choices described the Spirit's work of making us holy, which is also true, so they now describe earning forgiveness or righteousness by our own effort, which the catechism denies.

question: What comfort does the resurrection of the body offer you?
answer: Not only shall my soul after this life immediately be taken up to Christ, my Head, but also this my flesh, raised by the power of Christ, shall be reunited with my soul and made like Christ's glorious body.
right_choice: Soul goes to Christ; flesh is raised by His power, reunited with soul, made like His glorious body.
wrong_choices: My soul goes to heaven but my body remains sleeping in the earth eternally. | I will exist forever as a spirit in heaven completely without any body. | My body is raised purely spiritual and invisible, with no physical substance whatsoever.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What comfort do you receive from the article about the life everlasting?
answer: Since I now already feel in my heart the beginning of eternal joy, I shall after this life possess perfect blessedness, such as no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man conceived-- a blessedness in which to praise God forever.
right_choice: I already feel eternal joy's beginning in my heart; I will possess perfect blessedness beyond perception and praise God forever.
wrong_choices: I will someday reach perfect peace and joy when I depart from this world and enter God's presence | I will later enjoy perfect peace and happiness forever in the presence of God in the heavenly place | I feel no joy yet in this life; I will earn perfect blessedness after death by my own good works
audit_why: One wrong choice said almost what the catechism teaches (joy now, perfect blessedness later), so it was replaced with a choice that clearly contradicts it.

question: But what does it help you now that you believe all this?
answer: In Christ I am righteous before God and heir to life everlasting.
right_choice: In Christ I am righteous before God and heir to life everlasting.
wrong_choices: Through my faith in Christ I have earned my eternal life. | In Christ I am perfect in all my works and truly holy. | In Christ I am partially righteous and must hope for more righteousness.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How are you righteous before God?
answer: Only by true faith in Jesus Christ. Although my conscience accuses me that I have grievously sinned against all God's commandments, have never kept any of them, and am still inclined to all evil, yet God, without any merit of my own, out of mere grace, imputes to me the perfect satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ. He grants these to me as if I had never had nor committed any sin, and as if I myself had accomplished all the obedience which Christ has rendered for me, if only I accept this gift with a believing heart.
right_choice: Only by faith in Christ; God imputes Christ's satisfaction and righteousness to me as though I never sinned.
wrong_choices: By the work of the Holy Spirit making me righteous as I grow in holiness and obey God | By my genuine faith in Christ and by becoming increasingly righteous through moral effort and sincere obedience | By faith in Christ combined with my good works that show my sincere commitment to living a holy life
audit_why: The question and answer match the catechism and the Bible (Romans 3:21-28; 4:3-5), and the wrong choices are clearly wrong by that teaching; only the short right choice was too long, so it was trimmed.

question: Why do you say that you are righteous only by faith?
answer: Not that I am acceptable to God on account of the worthiness of my faith, for only the satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ is my righteousness before God. I can receive this righteousness and make it mine in no other way than by faith only.
right_choice: Not because faith itself is righteous, but Christ's satisfaction and righteousness are mine; I receive them by faith only.
wrong_choices: Because the worthiness of my faith makes me acceptable to God | Because my faith and my obedience together complete the righteousness Christ began | Because faith is a good work that earns God's favor alongside Christ's merits
audit_why: The answer had a typo and strayed from the catechism's wording, and two wrong choices were really true statements about faith, so I restored the catechism's wording and replaced them with choices that make faith itself the ground of righteousness.

question: But why can our good works not be our righteousness before God, or at least a part of it?
answer: Because the righteousness which can stand before God's judgment must be absolutely perfect and in complete agreement with the law of God, whereas even our best works in this life are all imperfect and defiled with sin.
right_choice: God's law requires perfect righteousness; our best works are imperfect and defiled.
wrong_choices: God's law applies only to the Old Testament and no longer binds us. | God forbids good works and wants us to rest from all labor. | Our works are imperfect but still count toward at least half of righteousness.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: But do our good works earn nothing, even though God promises to reward them in this life and the next?
answer: This reward is not earned; it is a gift of grace.
right_choice: This reward is not earned; it is a gift of grace.
wrong_choices: The reward for good works comes through our own merit and labor. | God rewards the godly for their works out of obligation to them. | God only rewards those who perfectly obey all of His commands.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Does this teaching not make people careless and wicked?
answer: No. It is impossible that those grafted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of thankfulness.
right_choice: No. It is impossible that those grafted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of thankfulness.
wrong_choices: Yes, many believers become careless about morality since they are assured that Christ paid for their sins | No, because good works must be done to earn God's favor, and that keeps people from becoming careless | No, but sincere believers must strive hard to produce good works to ensure they remain grafted into Christ
audit_why: One wrong choice (that believers may struggle to bear fruit) is true enough that it could also be chosen, so it was replaced with a choice that clearly contradicts salvation by grace.

question: Since then faith alone makes us share in Christ and all His benefits, where does this faith come from?
answer: From the Holy Spirit, who works it in our hearts by the preaching of the gospel, and strengthens it by the use of the sacraments.
right_choice: From the Holy Spirit, who works it by the gospel and strengthens it through the sacraments.
wrong_choices: From God's free choice and from our own personal decision to believe in Christ as our Savior | From our own good works and from the church's rituals that earn us a share in Christ's benefits | From our parents' faith and from Christian education that teaches us to believe in Jesus as our Lord
audit_why: One wrong choice (the Word of God and the Holy Spirit working through reason) was nearly the same as the catechism's answer, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong choice about earning faith by works and rituals.

question: What are the sacraments?
answer: The sacraments are holy, visible signs and seals. They were instituted by God so that by their use He might the more fully declare and seal to us the promise of the gospel. And this is the promise: that God graciously grants us forgiveness of sins and everlasting life because of the one sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross.
right_choice: Holy visible signs and seals instituted by God declaring and sealing forgiveness and eternal life through Christ's one sacrifice.
wrong_choices: Sacred ceremonies and rituals instituted by the church that remind us of Christ's work and Christian commitment | Holy means of grace established by Christ that mysteriously convey God's forgiveness and spiritual power to the faithful | Outward religious ceremonies that symbolize our faith in Christ and demonstrate our dedication to the Christian life
audit_why: The answer matches the Heidelberg Catechism, but the reference "Rom 4:1" should be Rom 4:11, where circumcision is called a sign and seal, so the reference was corrected.

question: According to the Heidelberg Catechism, what does the Holy Spirit teach us in the gospel and assure us by the sacraments that our entire salvation rests on?
answer: Christ's one sacrifice for us on the cross. The Holy Spirit teaches this in the gospel and assures us of it by the sacraments.
right_choice: Christ's one sacrifice for us on the cross
wrong_choices: Our own obedience to God's law and good works | Our growth in holiness through the Lord's Supper | The church's repeated offering of Christ in the sacraments
audit_why: The original wrong choices were also true (the Word and sacraments do point us to Christ), so the question now asks what our salvation rests on, with clearly wrong choices.

question: How many sacraments has Christ instituted in the new covenant?
answer: Two: holy baptism and the holy supper.
right_choice: Two: holy baptism and the holy supper.
wrong_choices: Seven: baptism, confirmation, penance, eucharist, unction, orders, and matrimony. | Three: baptism, the supper, and confirmation as practiced in the church. | One: only baptism, as the supper is merely a memorial meal.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How does holy baptism signify and seal to you that the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross benefits you?
answer: In this way: Christ instituted this outward washing and with it gave the promise that, as surely as water washes away the dirt from the body, so certainly His blood and Spirit wash away the impurity of my soul, that is, all my sins.
right_choice: Water in baptism washes dirt as His blood and Spirit wash away all my sins, Christ's promise at His institution.
wrong_choices: Just as water cleanses the body completely, so the sacrament of baptism miraculously removes all our sins | Water cleanses dirt from the body, and baptism through God's sacramental action miraculously cleanses our soul | Baptism is an outward sign that we have already been cleansed inwardly and commit ourselves to Christ
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What does it mean to be washed with Christ's blood and Spirit?
answer: To be washed with Christ's blood means to receive forgiveness of sins from God, through grace, because of Christ's blood, poured out for us in His sacrifice on the cross. To be washed with His Spirit means to be renewed by the Holy Spirit and sanctified to be members of Christ, so that more and more we become dead to sin and lead a holy and blameless life.
right_choice: Christ's blood washes away sins through grace; His Spirit renews and sanctifies us to live holy.
wrong_choices: Blood washes priests; Spirit washes believers; together they make us completely sinless. | Blood means outward cleansing; Spirit means inner peace and emotional comfort only. | Washed with blood means we never sin again; washed with Spirit means perfect knowledge.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Where has Christ promised that He will wash us with His blood and Spirit as surely as we are washed with the water of baptism?
answer: In the institution of baptism, where He says: “Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” and “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.” This promise is repeated where Scripture speaks of baptism as the washing of new birth and the washing away of sins.
right_choice: In the institution of baptism, a promise repeated where Scripture speaks of the washing of new birth
wrong_choices: In the story of His own baptism, where the Spirit descended on Him like a dove | In the Sermon on the Mount, where He promises that the pure in heart will see God | In the institution of the Lord’s Supper, where He tells us to eat the bread and drink the cup
audit_why: The answer used non-BSB wording (such as "He who believes" and "washing of regeneration"), and the wrong choices were all nearly the same as the right one, so the answer now quotes the BSB and the wrong choices name other places in Scripture.

question: Does this outward washing with water itself wash away sins?
answer: No, only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins.
right_choice: No, only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins.
wrong_choices: Yes, water washes sins away, while the Spirit provides additional grace and comfort. | Yes, water itself has cleansing power when used in baptism by a priest. | Yes, but only if the person being baptized has perfect faith and repentance.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why then does the Holy Spirit call baptism the washing of regeneration and the washing away of sins?
answer: God speaks in this way for a good reason. He wants to teach us that the blood and Spirit of Christ remove our sins just as water takes away dirt from the body. But, even more important, He wants to assure us by this divine pledge and sign that we are as truly cleansed from our sins spiritually as we are bodily washed with water.
right_choice: God teaches blood and Spirit remove sins like water removes dirt, and assures us we're truly cleansed spiritually as bodily.
wrong_choices: God declares that through baptism the water magically transforms us so that all our sins are completely erased | God wants us to know that baptism physically removes the stains of sin just as water removes dirt | The Holy Spirit teaches that baptism is a powerful means through which God actually cleanses us from sin
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Should infants, too, be baptized?
answer: Yes. Infants as well as adults belong to God's covenant and congregation. Through Christ's blood the redemption from sin and the Holy Spirit, who works faith, are promised to them no less than to adults. Therefore, by baptism, as sign of the covenant, they must be grafted into the Christian church and distinguished from the children of unbelievers. This was done in the old covenant by circumcision, in place of which baptism was instituted in the new covenant.
right_choice: Yes, infants belong to God's covenant and receive redemption and Spirit; baptism grafts them into the church replacing circumcision.
wrong_choices: Yes, because baptism itself washes away the sin they inherited from Adam and makes them children of God | Yes, infants must be baptized immediately so they can receive God's grace and be part of God's covenant | Yes, but only when both parents are church members, since the covenant promise belongs to them alone
audit_why: Two wrong choices were so close to the catechism's teaching (belonging to Christian parents, being marked as God's people) that they could be picked, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict it.

question: How does the Lord's Supper signify and seal to you that you share in Christ's one sacrifice on the cross and in all His gifts?
answer: In this way: Christ has commanded me and all believers to eat of this broken bread and drink of this cup in remembrance of Him. With this command He gave these promises: First, as surely as I see with my eyes the bread of the Lord broken for me and the cup given to me, so surely was His body offered for me and His blood poured out for me on the cross. Second, as surely as I receive from the hand of the minister and taste with my mouth the bread and the cup of the Lord as sure signs of Christ's body and blood, so surely does He Himself nourish and refresh my soul to everlasting life with His crucified body and shed blood.
right_choice: As surely as I receive bread and cup, so surely Christ was offered for me and nourishes my soul.
wrong_choices: As surely as I receive bread and cup, so surely the priest repeats Christ's sacrifice to earn my forgiveness | Christ commanded us to eat the bread and drink the cup to remember His death; these elements truly are His body and blood | Commands remembrance of His sacrifice through this sacred meal; the bread and wine are His actual flesh and blood present
audit_why: One wrong choice said Christ feeds our souls in the meal, which is just what the catechism teaches, so it was replaced with a wrong teaching (a repeated sacrifice), and the right choice was shortened and now includes the promise that Christ's body was offered for me.

question: What does it mean to eat the crucified body of Christ and to drink His shed blood?
answer: First, to accept with a believing heart all the suffering and the death of Christ, and so receive forgiveness of sins and life eternal. Second, to be united more and more to His sacred body through the Holy Spirit, who lives both in Christ and in us. Therefore, although Christ is in heaven and we are on earth, yet we are flesh of His flesh and bone of His bones, and we forever live and are governed by one Spirit, as the members of our body are by one soul.
right_choice: To accept Christ's suffering and death for forgiveness and be united with His body through the Spirit.
wrong_choices: To believe that Christ's literal body is present in the bread and wine through the priest's blessing. | To accept Christ's suffering by faith while remaining spiritually separate from His body until heaven. | To commemorate Christ's death through eating bread and wine as reminders and symbols only.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Where has Christ promised that He will nourish and refresh believers with His body and blood as surely as they eat of this broken bread and drink of this cup?
answer: In the institution of the Lord's Supper: "The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread, and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, 'This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.' In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.' For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes." Paul repeats this promise: "Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf."
right_choice: At the institution of the Lord's Supper, and in Paul's words on sharing in Christ's body and blood.
wrong_choices: At Pentecost when the Holy Spirit was given to believers at the breaking of bread. | In the feeding of the five thousand where Christ multiplied loaves and fishes for the multitude. | At the Transfiguration where Christ was glorified with Moses and Elijah, eating and drinking with them.
audit_why: The Bible quotations in the answer now follow the BSB word for word (including "This cup is the new covenant in My blood" and "one loaf"), and the right choice is shortened so it fits the limit and no longer stands out.

question: Are then the bread and wine changed into the real body and blood of Christ?
answer: No. Just as the water of baptism is not changed into the blood of Christ and is not the washing away of sins itself but is simply God's sign and pledge, so also the bread in the Lord's supper does not become the body of Christ itself, although it is called Christ's body in keeping with the nature and usage of sacraments.
right_choice: No. Water isn't changed to blood in baptism; bread isn't changed to body in supper but is called so sacramentally.
wrong_choices: Yes. Through the priest's consecration the bread is transformed into the real body of Christ. | No. But the bread becomes Christ's body through God's power even though nothing appears to change. | Yes. Though it remains bread in appearance, the substance is miraculously changed into Christ's body.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why then does Christ call the bread His body and the cup His blood, or the new covenant in His blood, and why does Paul speak of a participation in the body and blood of Christ?
answer: Christ speaks in this way for a good reason: He wants to teach us by His supper that as bread and wine sustain us in this temporal life, so His crucified body and shed blood are true food and drink for our souls to eternal life. But, even more important, He wants to assure us by this visible sign and pledge, first, that through the working of the Holy Spirit we share in His true body and blood as surely as we receive with our mouth these holy signs in remembrance of Him, and, second, that all His suffering and obedience are as certainly ours as if we personally had suffered and paid for our sins.
right_choice: Bread nourishes bodies as His body nourishes souls eternally; by Spirit we truly share in Him and His suffering becomes ours.
wrong_choices: The bread and wine are merely symbols of Christ's body and blood with no real spiritual significance to believers | The bread and wine physically transform into His body and blood through the priest's consecration for literal consumption | Through priestly blessing, Christ's body is daily re-offered for the sins of both living and dead
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What difference is there between the Lord's supper and the papal mass?
answer: The Lord's supper testifies to us, first, that we have complete forgiveness of all our sins through the one sacrifice of Jesus Christ, which He Himself accomplished on the cross once for all; and, second, that through the Holy Spirit we are grafted into Christ, who with His true body is now in heaven at the right hand of the Father, and this is where He wants to be worshipped. But the mass teaches, first, that the living and the dead do not have forgiveness of sins through the suffering of Christ unless He is still offered for them daily by the priests; and, second, that Christ is bodily present in the form of bread and wine, and there is to be worshipped. Therefore the mass is basically nothing but a denial of the one sacrifice and suffering of Jesus Christ, and an accursed idolatry.
right_choice: Supper witnesses complete forgiveness through Christ's one sacrifice; mass wrongly teaches daily re-offering and worship of Christ bodily present in bread.
wrong_choices: Both Supper and mass teach that Christ is present in the bread and wine to be worshipped by believers | The Lord's Supper teaches that forgiveness needs daily offering by priests, while the mass rests on Christ's one sacrifice on the cross | The Lord's Supper and the mass are essentially the same, both offering Christ's sacrifice daily for the living and dead
audit_why: One wrong choice described what the mass teaches, which matches the catechism, so I replaced it with a reversed statement that is clearly wrong.

question: Who are to come to the table of the Lord?
answer: Those who are truly displeased with themselves because of their sins and yet trust that these are forgiven them and that their remaining weakness is covered by the suffering and death of Christ, and who also desire more and more to strengthen their faith and amend their life. But hypocrites and those who do not repent eat and drink judgment upon themselves.
right_choice: Those displeased with their sins who trust Christ's death covers them and want to strengthen faith and amend life.
wrong_choices: Only the spiritually mature and morally pure who have overcome their greatest temptations and weaknesses. | All baptized members of the Christian church who profess belief in Christ and are confirmed communicants. | Those who have confessed their sins to the minister and promise to endeavor to live better.
audit_why: The catechism answer is right, but the reference now cites only 1 Corinthians 11:26-32, since 10:19-22 is about the table of demons, and the short right choice is trimmed to fit the length limit.

question: Are those also to be admitted to the Lord's supper who by their confession and life show that they are unbelieving and ungodly?
answer: No, for then the covenant of God would be profaned and His wrath kindled against the whole congregation. Therefore, according to the command of Christ and His apostles, the Christian church is duty-bound to exclude such persons by the keys of the kingdom of heaven, until they amend their lives.
right_choice: No. The covenant would be profaned and God's wrath kindled. The church must exclude them by ecclesiastical discipline.
wrong_choices: No, but the church should admit them secretly to avoid seeming harsh or judgmental toward them. | Yes. The supper should be offered to all as a means toward their eventual conversion. | Only if they refuse to repent; those showing some signs of faith should be permitted.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What are the keys of the kingdom of heaven?
answer: The preaching of the holy gospel and church discipline. By these two the kingdom of heaven is opened to believers and closed to unbelievers.
right_choice: Gospel preaching and church discipline. These open the kingdom to believers and close it to unbelievers.
wrong_choices: The authority of priests alone to forgive sins and administer the sacraments to cleanse the congregation | The apostle Peter alone, to whom Christ gave the exclusive keys to bind and loose all sins eternally | Prayer and fasting by the church leaders, by which the kingdom is spiritually opened to the worthy
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How is the kingdom of heaven opened and closed by the preaching of the gospel?
answer: According to the command of Christ, the kingdom of heaven is opened when it is proclaimed and publicly testified to each and every believer that God has really forgiven all their sins for the sake of Christ's merits, as often as they by true faith accept the promise of the gospel. The kingdom of heaven is closed when it is proclaimed and testified to all unbelievers and hypocrites that the wrath of God and eternal condemnation rest on them as long as they do not repent. According to this testimony of the gospel, God will judge both in this life and in the life to come.
right_choice: It opens by proclaiming God's forgiveness to believers and closes by proclaiming His wrath on unrepentant unbelievers.
wrong_choices: The gospel proclaims forgiveness to all people indiscriminately, promising that God's love prevents any from experiencing His eternal wrath | The gospel declares that believers receive automatic forgiveness without repentance, while unbelievers face eternal separation from God's presence | Gospel preaching by the church opens the kingdom only to those who receive the sacraments from authorized priests
audit_why: The catechism answer and the wrong choices are sound, but the short right choice was one word too long, so it was reworded more briefly with the same meaning.

question: How is the kingdom of heaven closed and opened by church discipline?
answer: According to the command of Christ, people who call themselves Christians but show themselves to be unchristian in doctrine or life are first repeatedly admonished in a brotherly manner. If they do not give up their errors or wickedness, they are reported to the church, that is, to the elders. If they do not heed also their admonitions, they are forbidden the use of the sacraments, and they are excluded by the elders from the Christian congregation, and by God Himself from the kingdom of Christ. They are again received as members of Christ and of the church when they promise and show real amendment.
right_choice: Unchristian members are admonished, reported to elders, forbidden sacraments, and excluded. They're received back when they show real amendment.
wrong_choices: Church discipline immediately excommunicates those who sin without any chance for repentance or restoration to the church community | Members showing unchristian behavior should be privately criticized by elders but allowed to continue receiving all church sacraments | Sinful church members are permanently barred from the church once admonished, never permitted to return regardless of their later repentance
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Since we have been delivered from our misery by grace alone through Christ, without any merit of our own, why must we yet do good works?
answer: Because Christ, having redeemed us by His blood, also renews us by His Holy Spirit to be His image, so that with our whole life we may show ourselves thankful to God for His benefits, and He may be praised by us. Further, that we ourselves may be assured of our faith by its fruits, and that by our godly walk of life we may win our neighbours for Christ.
right_choice: Show thankfulness to God and praise Him; assure ourselves of faith by its fruits; win neighbors to Christ by godly living.
wrong_choices: We do good works because Christ's redemption obligates us to keep God's law perfectly to maintain our salvation | Good works are necessary to earn God's favor, since our justification depends on the quality of our righteous deeds | Good works are optional displays of superior piety for Christians, but are not required by God for any believer
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Can those be saved who do not turn to God from their ungrateful and impenitent walk of life?
answer: By no means. Scripture says that no unchaste person, idolater, adulterer, thief, greedy person, drunkard, slanderer, robber, or the like shall inherit the kingdom of God.
right_choice: By no means. No unchaste person, idolater, adulterer, thief, greedy person, drunkard, slanderer, or robber shall inherit God's kingdom.
wrong_choices: Only those who refuse to turn are lost; those who once believed keep their salvation. | Yes. God's mercy and Christ's sacrifice forgive all sins regardless of the sinner's repentance. | Yes. If they have faith alone they will be saved despite their continued impenitent lifestyle.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is the true repentance or conversion of man?
answer: It is the dying of the old nature and the coming to life of the new.
right_choice: It is the dying of the old nature and the coming to life of the new.
wrong_choices: Repentance is confessing our sins to a priest and receiving his absolution. | Repentance is obeying God's law perfectly for the rest of our life on earth. | Repentance is making satisfaction and payment to God for our sinful acts.
audit_why: One wrong choice, sorrow for sin, is part of what the catechism calls the dying of the old nature, so it was replaced with a choice that is clearly wrong.

question: What is the dying of the old nature?
answer: It is to grieve with heartfelt sorrow that we have offended God by our sin, and more and more to hate it and flee from it.
right_choice: To grieve with heartfelt sorrow that we offended God by sin, and increasingly to hate and flee from it.
wrong_choices: To feel deep regret for the consequences of sin but without necessarily rejecting sin itself as offensive to God | To recognize that sinning is wrong in theory while continuing to practice sin with an understanding that grace covers it | To temporarily mourn one's sins while aware they will be forgiven, and then gradually to move beyond the grief
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is the coming to life of the new nature?
answer: It is a heartfelt joy in God through Christ, and a love and delight to live according to the will of God in all good works.
